en: The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Five Ungrateful Acts, translated by the Song dynasty layman Juqu Jingsheng.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī with twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

At that time, there was a brahmin who came from the kingdom of Rājagṛha. Having heard that the people of Śrāvastī were compassionate, filial, and obedient, that they upheld the sūtras and cultivated the Way, and that they reverently served the Three Honored Ones, he then arrived in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
He saw a father and son plowing a field when a venomous snake bit and killed the son; yet the father continued to plow without looking at his son, nor did he weep.
A brahmin asked, "Whose son is this?"
The plowman replied, "He is my son. The brahmin asked:
"This is your son; why does he not weep? Why do you continue to plow as before?

The man replied, "In human life there is death, and for things that come to fruition there is decay. For the good there is retribution, and for the evil there is its counterpart. What benefit is there in sorrow, lack of joy, weeping, or lamentation for one who has died?"
"As you enter the city today, at such-and-such a place in my house, I wish for you to go and tell them:
'My son has already died; simply bring food for one person!
The Brahmin thought to himself:
“Who is this person, devoid of gratitude? While his son lies dead upon the ground, he feels no sorrow; instead, he seeks food!
This man lacks compassion; there is no comparison to such a person!”
The brahmin entered the city and went to the house of the plowman; seeing the mother of the deceased child, he immediately said:
"Your son has died. His father sends this message: bring food for but one person."
"Why do you not think of your son?
The mother of the child then spoke a parable for the brahmin, saying:
"When my son came to be conceived in me, I did not call him; now that he is departing of his own accord, it is not within my power to retain him."
It is like a traveler who comes to visit a host; once the guest has departed on their own, how can they be detained? My mother and I are just the same:

our going or staying, our advancing or halting, are not within my power. We must follow our own past karma and cannot remain; what benefit is there in grieving, weeping, and lamenting for one who is dead?
He spoke again to his sister, saying, "Your brother is already dead; why do you not weep?
The sister then spoke a parable for the Brahmin:

"My brothers are like skilled craftsmen who enter the mountains to fell timber and bind it together to make a great raft. Having placed it upon the water, they were suddenly struck by a great wind that blew the raft apart and scattered it; carried away by the current, the pieces drifted apart, neither looking back at the others. My younger brother was just the same:

though we met through the convergence of causes and conditions and were born into the same family, according to the length of our lives, birth and death are impermanent; where there is meeting, there must be parting."
"My younger brother's life has ended; according to his past karma, he cannot be retained. What benefit is there in grieving and weeping for one who is dead?
He then spoke again to his wife:
"Your husband is already dead; why do you not weep?"
The wife spoke this parable for the brahmin:

"My husband and I are like flying birds that roost together upon a high tree at nightfall; after a short while, when dawn breaks and they rise, each flies away in search of food and drink. They reunite when there is a cause for it, and part when there is no cause.

My husband and I are just the same: our going and staying, our advancing and halting, are not within my power; we follow our own past karma and cannot remain together. What benefit is there in grieving, worrying, or weeping for one who is dead?"
He spoke again to the slave:
"The master has died; why do you not weep?
The slave then spoke a parable for the Brahmin:

"My master, through the convergence of causes and conditions, was like a great bull that I, like a calf, followed. When people killed the great bull, I, the calf, remained by his side; though I could not save the life of the great bull, I am sorrowful and unhappy, weeping and distressed. What benefit is there in grieving for one who has died?"
Upon hearing this, the brahmin’s mind was bewildered and his vision darkened; he could no longer distinguish east from west, thinking:
"I heard that this country is filial and obedient, and that its people serve and revere the Triple Gem. Therefore, I came from afar desiring to study and learn;
yet now that I have arrived here, it has proven to be of no benefit at all."
He further asked the practitioner,
"Where is the Buddha?
I wish to go and question him."
The practitioner replied, "He is nearby at the Jeta Grove Monastery.
The brahmin immediately went to the Buddha's location, prostrated himself in greeting, and withdrew to stand to one side; with a sorrowful face and bowed head, he remained silent and spoke no word.
The Buddha, knowing his thoughts, said to the brahmin:
"Why do you lower your head, appearing sorrowful and unhappy?
The brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Because my wishes have not been fulfilled and they contradict my original intention, I am unhappy!
The Buddha asked the brahmin:
“What have you lost that causes you such sorrow and unhappiness?”
The brahmin said:
"I have come from the kingdom of Rājagṛha, desiring to pursue learning;
having arrived here, I have observed five things that show no gratitude."
The Buddha asked,
"What are the five kinds of ingratitude?
The brahmin replied:

"I saw a father and son plowing the earth and sowing seeds; when the son died in the field, the father felt no sorrow and instead went out to seek food, and the members of his household, both great and small, likewise felt no grief—this is a grave act of rebellion."
The Buddha said, "It is not so!
It is not as you have said."
These five people are the most resilient;
they know that the body is impermanent and that wealth does not belong to oneself. Even the sages of antiquity could not escape this affliction, let alone ordinary beings.
What benefit is there in loud wailing and small weeping for one who has died?

Since beginningless kalpas, worldly people have transmigrated through birth and death; their spirits shift without perishing, dying and being born again like the turning of a wheel, never resting. Turning away from death toward life is not something that sorrow can reach.
Upon hearing this, the brahmin’s mind was opened and his understanding attained; he was no longer troubled by grief, thinking:
"Hearing the Buddha's teaching is like a sick person being cured, like a blind person regaining sight, or like encountering light in the darkness."
Thereupon, the brahmin immediately attained the fruit of the Path.

"All death is not worth weeping for; rather, for one who has passed away, it is most essential to invite the Buddha and the Sangha, to burn incense and make offerings, to recite the scriptures, to pay homage day after day, and to further make offerings with a sincere heart to the Triple Gem."
Thereupon, the brahmin bowed his head in prostration, received the instruction, and departed.
Thus ends the *Buddha-bhāṣita-pañca-anupakārin-sūtra*.
